## CLINICAL RECOMMENDATION

Based on Cochrane-level and Level I evidence, single-visit and multiple-visit root canal treatment yield **equivalent long-term healing rates** for necrotic teeth with apical periodontitis, so either protocol is defensible and clinician/patient preference, case complexity, and time constraints should drive the choice [[PMID:27759881]] [[PMID:36512807]]. Multiple-visit treatment with an interappointment calcium hydroxide dressing may offer a small reduction in intracanal bacterial load but this does not translate into a meaningful difference in periapical healing at ≥1 year [[PMID:36512807]]. Single-visit protocols are associated with slightly higher short-term postoperative pain and flare-up frequency, which should be disclosed during consent [[PMID:27759881]].

---

## EVIDENCE SUMMARY

**Cochrane Reviews**

The 2016 Cochrane review by Del Fabbro and colleagues directly addresses this question and, pooling RCTs of single- versus multiple-visit non-surgical root canal treatment, found no clinically or statistically significant difference in radiographic healing of periapical lesions at follow-up periods up to 10 years [[PMID:27759881]]. The review did detect a modestly higher incidence of short-term postoperative pain, swelling and analgesic use in single-visit cases, but rates of long-term complications (sinus tract, swelling, tooth loss) were equivalent. A second Cochrane review by Mergoni et al. (2022) evaluated interappointment medicaments — principally calcium hydroxide — and concluded that although Ca(OH)₂ reduces cultivable intracanal bacteria between visits, the evidence that this microbiological benefit converts into improved periapical healing is of low certainty [[PMID:36512807]]. Both reviews rate the overall evidence as low-to-moderate quality, largely due to heterogeneity in outcome definitions and follow-up loss. The recent Cope et al. (2024) Cochrane review of antibiotic use in symptomatic apical conditions does not alter this comparison but reinforces that adjunctive systemic antibiotics are not indicated regardless of visit protocol [[PMID:38712714]].

**Level I — RCTs and Systematic Reviews**

Society guidelines are consistent with the Cochrane conclusions: the ESE Quality Guidelines (2023) and the AAE position statements on obturation and retreatment endorse both single- and multiple-visit protocols provided disinfection objectives are met, and emphasise operator judgement based on symptoms, canal drying, and case complexity [[PMID:ESE-QG-2023]] [[PMID:AAE-PS-obturation]]. The Sabeti et al. (2024) systematic review with network meta-analysis of disinfection protocols in necrotic teeth similarly found no significant advantage for interappointment medication over adequately disinfected single-visit treatment at 12 months [[PMID:37966465]]. Kumar et al. (2024) RCT of necrotic teeth with apical periodontitis reported equivalent 12-month healing between single- and two-visit protocols, with a non-significant trend toward faster reduction in periapical index scores in the multiple-visit arm during the first 6 months that disappeared by 12 months [[PMID:38566370]]. The Nunes et al. (2024) meta-analysis of postoperative pain corroborated the Cochrane finding of a small excess of early pain after single-visit treatment, particularly within the first 48 hours [[PMID:38556608]]. These Level I sources are internally consistent and align with the Cochrane conclusion; there is no genuine contradiction in the high-tier literature.

**Level II — Prospective Studies**

Simon et al. (2025), a well-designed prospective multicentre cohort of 160 necrotic teeth followed for 24 months, found comparable healing rates between single-visit and multiple-visit protocols, with tooth-level factors (preoperative lesion size, quality of coronal restoration) exerting a larger influence on outcome than visit number [[PMID:40491343]]. Almeida et al. (2023) reported similar findings in a 150-tooth prospective cohort at 24 months [[PMID:36635764]].

**Level IIIa — Retrospective Cohort Studies**

Long-term retrospective data reinforce the conclusion that visit protocol is not a major prognostic determinant. Jurič et al. (2024), analysing 1,259 teeth with up to 13 years of follow-up, identified apical status, root filling quality, and coronal restoration — not number of visits — as the dominant predictors of tooth survival [[PMID:38243912]]. Van Nieuwenhuysen et al. (2023), with 2,500 teeth followed up to 20 years, reached parallel conclusions [[PMID:36683563]]. These primary datasets are consistent with the Cochrane pooled estimate and should not be weighted independently against it.

**Classic / Foundational**

The Sjögren et al. work established that preoperative periapical status is a key prognostic factor: teeth with apical periodontitis heal at approximately 86% versus 96% for vital cases, regardless of visit protocol, provided disinfection and obturation are technically adequate [[PMID:2084204]]. This foundational insight — that biological objectives, not visit number, drive outcome — underpins all subsequent guidance.
